quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Travel Expense Policy] Employees may claim reasonable travel costs for approved business trips. Flights must be booked in economy class at least 14 days in advance; last-minute bookings require written approval from a director. Hotel stays are reimbursed up to $140 per night, and any amount above that is paid by the employee. Meals are covered at a flat rate of $45 per day, with no receipts needed, but alcohol is never reimbursed. Claims must be submitted within 30 days of returning; claims submitted later will be considered only in exceptional circumstances. Employees who extend a trip for personal reasons must pay for the extra nights themselves.
quests.question: An employee books a flight 10 days before a trip. What does she need?
options: A receipt for the ticket
A letter from the hotel
Written approval from a director
Permission from a colleague
quests.correctAnswer: Written approval from a director
quests.hint: Compare 10 days with the minimum advance time in the policy.
quests.explanation: Flights must be booked at least 14 days ahead, so a booking made 10 days before counts as last-minute and needs a director's written approval.
quests.evidenceLine: last-minute bookings require written approval from a director

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Cities Run Hot] On a summer evening, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while tall buildings block cooling breezes. A scarcity of trees makes matters worse, since leaves shade the ground and release water vapor that cools the air. In one study, streets lined with mature trees were up to six degrees cooler than similar streets without them. Planners increasingly favor planting trees and painting roofs white, though a few residents complain that the work causes disruption and that trees can block shop signs.
quests.question: According to the passage, why do dark surfaces keep cities warm at night?
options: They reflect most sunlight back up into the sky.
They release stored heat slowly after sunset.
They block the cooling breezes from the countryside.
They give off water vapor through the night.
quests.correctAnswer: They release stored heat slowly after sunset.
quests.hint: Follow what happens to sunlight during the day and then after dark.
quests.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb sunlight by day and let the heat out slowly once the sun has set.
quests.evidenceLine: absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly after sunset

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Last Lesson] Mr. Okafor had taught chemistry for thirty-one years, and on his last day he did what he always did: he wrote the date on the board, checked that the burners were off, and began the lesson. The students, who had planned a small party, waited. Halfway through, he stopped and looked at the clock. "I had a speech prepared," he said. "But I notice it's ten past two, and you have a test tomorrow." Someone groaned. He smiled, picked up the chalk, and carried on. Only when the bell rang did he turn to them, glance at the cake on the back bench, and say, "Now, I think there was something about a party."
quests.question: What does Mr. Okafor's decision to continue the lesson suggest about him?
options: He values his routine and his students' preparation.
He dislikes parties and wants to avoid this one.
He completely forgot about the planned party.
He is angry with the class for planning a party.
quests.correctAnswer: He values his routine and his students' preparation.
quests.hint: Consider his reason for skipping the speech.
quests.explanation: He puts the test the next day ahead of the speech, which shows how seriously he takes teaching.
quests.evidenceLine: I notice it's ten past two, and you have a test tomorrow

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [A Note from the Owner] Many of you have asked why Tomo's Kitchen will now be closed on Mondays. The short answer is that I could not keep going the way I was. For eight years I worked seven days a week, and last winter I realized that the food I was most proud of was not coming out of a kitchen run by someone exhausted. I have also noticed that Monday is our quietest night, so closing costs us little. Our staff will now have a guaranteed day off, and I hope that happier cooks will repay you in better dinners. I understand if this is inconvenient. I would rather lose a few Monday customers than the quality that made you come in the first place.
quests.question: What is the owner's main purpose in writing?
options: To announce new prices
To advertise a Monday special
To apologize for poor service
To explain a change in opening days
quests.correctAnswer: To explain a change in opening days
quests.hint: Look at the question the note answers in its first sentence.
quests.explanation: The note opens with the question of why the restaurant will close on Mondays and spends the rest explaining the decision.
quests.evidenceLine: Many of you have asked why Tomo's Kitchen will now be closed on Mondays

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [E-reader or Paperback?] The case for the e-reader is practical: a single device holds hundreds of books, weighs less than a paperback, and lets you enlarge the print. For travelers and readers with poor eyesight, these advantages are real. Paperback defenders, however, point to something harder to measure. They say that a printed book makes it easier to remember where in the story a passage appeared, and that it comes without notifications or the temptation to check messages. There is some evidence for the first claim, but the second depends entirely on self-discipline, since most e-readers do not have notifications at all. The honest conclusion is that neither format is better; each simply suits a different kind of reader.
quests.question: Which statement best summarizes the writer's conclusion?
options: E-readers are better than paperbacks in every way.
Paperbacks are better than e-readers in every way.
Neither format is superior; it depends on the reader.
Readers should avoid both formats if they can.
quests.correctAnswer: Neither format is superior; it depends on the reader.
quests.hint: The last sentence states the writer's overall view.
quests.explanation: The writer concludes that neither format is better and that each suits a different kind of reader.
quests.evidenceLine: neither format is better; each simply suits a different kind of reader

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [School Phone Ban] Beginning in January, Harbourview High will require students to leave phones in locked pouches during the school day. Some parents are unconvinced. "I understand the problem," said one parent, "but I want to be able to reach my son if there's an emergency." The school says that office staff will pass urgent messages to students immediately, and that exceptions will be made for medical needs. A review of the policy is planned for June.

A survey showing most parents at Harbourview support the ban
A rise in test scores at Harbourview since phones were limited
Complaints from teachers at Harbourview about classroom noise
quests.correctAnswer: A trial at another school improved assignment completion.
quests.hint: Look for the result of a trial mentioned in the second sentence.
quests.explanation: The principal points to a neighboring school where more students finished assignments on time after a similar trial.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Community Grant Guidelines] Grants of up to $5,000 are available to registered community groups for projects that benefit local residents. To be eligible, a group must have been operating for at least one year and must contribute at least 20 percent of the project cost from its own funds or through donated services. Applications that request money for ongoing running costs, such as rent or salaries, will not be considered; one-time purchases, repairs and events are acceptable. Groups that received a grant last year may apply again only if they submitted a completed report on how the money was spent. Decisions are announced eight weeks after the closing date.

quests.hint: Find 20 percent of the total project cost.
quests.explanation: Twenty percent of $4,000 is $800, which the group must provide from its own funds or donated services.
quests.evidenceLine: at least 20 percent of the project cost

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [What the Garage Taught Me] My father's garage was never organized, but he could always find what he needed. Ask for a particular washer and he would move three boxes, reach behind a shelf, and produce it. As a teenager, I thought this was luck. After he died, I spent a weekend clearing the garage and discovered that nothing was where it looked. Each cluttered shelf hid a small, careful system: screws sorted by length inside old coffee tins, and the tins labeled in pencil on the underside, where only he would look. I did not tidy it in the end. I only added a label of my own, in the same place, in my own handwriting.
quests.question: What does the writer discover about the garage?
options: It was full of valuable items worth selling.
The apparent mess concealed a personal system.
It had been organized by a neighbor years earlier.
It contained almost no tools worth keeping.
quests.correctAnswer: The apparent mess concealed a personal system.
quests.hint: Look at the sentence that begins "Each cluttered shelf".
quests.explanation: Behind the clutter the writer found carefully sorted and labeled screws, which explains why the father could always find things.
quests.evidenceLine: Each cluttered shelf hid a small, careful system

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Coffee Costs What It Costs] A cup of coffee at a downtown café may cost twice as much as the same drink two miles away, and the beans are rarely the reason. Rent in busy districts can account for more of the price than the coffee itself, and cafés there must also pay higher wages to attract staff. Owners also consider what customers will accept: commuters buying a drink on the way to work are less price-sensitive than students lingering over a laptop. Some cafés therefore charge for the speed and convenience of the location rather than for the drink. Customers who walk an extra few blocks often find the same coffee for far less, which is why the cheapest cup is rarely the nearest one.
quests.question: According to the passage, what is the main reason downtown coffee costs more?
options: Better quality beans
More expensive milk
Higher rent and wages
Larger cups
quests.correctAnswer: Higher rent and wages
quests.hint: The first sentence says what is not the reason; the second explains the real one.
quests.explanation: Rent in busy districts and higher wages account for much of the price, rather than the beans.
quests.evidenceLine: Rent in busy districts can account for more of the price than the coffee itself

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Coffee Costs What It Costs] A cup of coffee at a downtown café may cost twice as much as the same drink two miles away, and the beans are rarely the reason. Rent in busy districts can account for more of the price than the coffee itself, and cafés there must also pay higher wages to attract staff. Owners also consider what customers will accept: commuters buying a drink on the way to work are less price-sensitive than students lingering over a laptop. Some cafés therefore charge for the speed and convenience of the location rather than for the drink. Customers who walk an extra few blocks often find the same coffee for far less, which is why the cheapest cup is rarely the nearest one.
quests.question: What advice can be drawn from the final sentence?
options: Walking a few blocks farther may save money.
Always buy coffee downtown.
Avoid cafés where people use laptops.
Buy beans instead of cups of coffee.
quests.correctAnswer: Walking a few blocks farther may save money.
quests.hint: The last sentence describes what customers who walk farther often find.
quests.explanation: Customers who walk a little farther often find the same coffee for far less.
quests.evidenceLine: walk an extra few blocks often find the same coffee for far less
